desc:
A board is given as an integer matrix grid, where 0 is a free cell and 1 is a hole. A domino covers exactly two free cells that share a side (it may lie horizontally or vertically).

Count the ways to place dominoes so that every free cell is covered by exactly one domino and no domino touches a hole. Two ways are different when the sets of dominoes differ. A board with no free cell at all has exactly one way (place nothing).

For example, a free 2 x 3 board has 3 tilings, and a free 2 x 2 board has 2.
hints: Look at the first free cell in row-major order (top row first, left to right). Whatever tiling you build, some domino must cover that cell.
That domino can only go to the right or down: the cell above and the cell to the left are either holes or already covered (they come earlier in the order). So there are at most 2 choices per step.

Keep an occupancy bitmask of all cells that are covered or are holes. Find the lowest empty bit, try the two placements that are possible, recurse, and add the counts. When no empty cell is left, return 1.
editorial: Always completing the first uncovered cell removes all symmetry: each tiling is produced exactly once, because the domino over the first free cell is forced to extend to the right or downward. A bitmask filled in row-major order holds holes and covered cells; low = ~filled & (filled + 1) isolates the first empty cell. A horizontal domino needs the next bit empty and the cell to stay in the same row, a vertical one needs the bit one row below to be empty and inside the board.

The number of search nodes is about the number of partial tilings that are still extendable. A full 6 x 6 board has 6,728 tilings, which is fast. A broken-profile dynamic programme (storing the occupancy of the next n cells) would count much larger boards in polynomial time per row, but the 36-cell limit lets plain backtracking pass.
